advances: Arbitrary finite sampling at three unequally spaced collinear sites. The measure counts only the sampled planes.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The two interpolating slopes are $1400/19$ and $50/1881$, positive and decreasing. The set of $(z,x,y)$ with $x,y\ge0$ and $x+y\le r(z)$ is convex by concavity and contains the listed fibers. On each interpolation interval, a convex combination of two of those lifted fibers fills its indicated section because Minkowski averages of homothetic copies of $T$ add their scales. Thus the stated sections are actual. Their sampled areas are $25/722,1/2,1521/2888$, giving $M$.

At $z=t$, use the three closed caps
$$-x-y-2(z-t)\ge-12/19,\qquad x-2(z-t)\ge6/19,\qquad y-2(z-t)\ge6/19.$$
Their margins sum to zero on $z=t$, so they cover that plane. At $z=0$ the first contains the entire first fiber and the other two miss it: $5/19<12/19+1/50$ and $5/19<6/19-1/50$. At $z=1$ the first threshold for $-x-y$ exceeds zero and the other two thresholds exceed $39/38$, so all miss the last fiber. At $z=t$ the three triangular cap areas are $(12/19)^2/2=144/722$ and $(1-6/19)^2/2=169/722$ twice. Each total sampled mass is therefore $Q$.

At $z=0$ use
$$-x-y-100z\ge-10/57,\qquad x-100z\ge5/57,\qquad y-100z\ge5/57.$$
Their margins sum to zero on that plane. The largest left sides on the middle fiber are $-1,0,0$, strictly below the corresponding thresholds, and the last fiber also misses them since the tilt there is $-100$ and its radius is $39/38$. Each first-fiber area is $(10/57)^2/2=50/3249<Q$.

At $z=1$ use
$$-x-y+2(z-1)\ge-13/19,\qquad x+2(z-1)\ge13/38,\qquad y+2(z-1)\ge13/38.$$
Their margins again sum to zero on the target plane. On the middle fiber the maxima of the left sides are $-99/50,1-99/50,1-99/50$, strictly below the thresholds. The maxima at the first base are even smaller. The last-fiber areas are all $(13/19)^2/2=Q$. Thus every point of every sampled fiber is contained in a closed cap of mass at most $Q$.

Conversely the last-fiber centroid is $(1,13/38,13/38)$. With $s=0$ the ordinary centroid inequality in 6a7d56e450b3126f gives mass at least $(4/9)(1521/2888)=Q$ on the last fiber in every oblique containing cap, using a parallel through-centroid cap inside it. A containing pure-base cap contains the whole fiber. This proves exact maximal depth. Convex traces on the three ordered sites are intervals. For an empty intersection of nonempty traces, the greatest first site and smallest last site already give two disjoint traces, while disjoint singletons show two are needed. Finally the exact ratio and gap follow by division. Scaling the base to $\{0,1,100\}$ and counting all integer sections would add the positive sections at $2,\ldots,99$.

statement: Let $T=\{(x,y):x,y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}$, $t=1/100$, and $P=\{0,t,1\}$. Take the lifted convex hull of the fibers $(5/19)T,T,(39/38)T$ at these bases. Its actual section is $r(z)T$ for every $z\in[0,1]$, where $r$ is the increasing positive concave piecewise affine interpolation of the three radii. On the three sampled planes only, use the sum of their two-dimensional Lebesgue measures, of total mass $M=3065/2888$, and test all closed ambient halfspaces. The exact raw maximum depth on the sampled union is $Q=169/722$, hence the normalized maximum is $676/3065<2/9=\Gamma_2/h(P)$, with gap $46/27585$. Here $h(P)=2$ is the Helly number of convex traces on $P$.
title: An exact finite-sampling depth obstruction with common-vertex simplex fibers
